messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Uncertainty: Uncertainty, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Duy is a 24-year-old house painter who came to therapy three months after the end of a two-year relationship with his ex-boyfriend, Marcus. The physical abuse had started slowly—a hard grip on his arm during an argument, a shove when Duy questioned him—but escalated one night in the apartment they shared. Duy had come home late from a job, paint still under his nails, and Marcus was waiting in the dark kitchen. He accused Duy of cheating. Duy tried to explain, but Marcus grabbed him by the throat and slammed his head against the refrigerator door. Duy remembers the cold metal against his scalp, the pressure on his windpipe, and then a series of disjointed images: the kitchen floor tiles, the edge of the counter, Marcus’s face twisted and red. He cannot put the sequence in order. Some moments—the sound of his own choked breathing, the way the refrigerator hummed—are excruciatingly clear. Others are completely blank, as if the tape was cut. He remembers Marcus letting go and walking away, and Duy lying on the floor, gasping, unable to move. That night, for the first time, he felt that he no longer belonged anywhere—not in that apartment, not in the relationship, not in his own life.

In the weeks that followed, Duy ended the relationship and moved into a small studio alone. But the memory did not stay in the past. When he lies in bed at night, the sound of a door closing or a floorboard creaking will yank him back into that kitchen. For a few seconds he is inside the moment again—his throat tight, his heart pounding, the helplessness flooding through him as if Marcus is still there. He has learned to avoid times of day that tend to bring on these episodes: late evenings, when the light is just like it was that night. He stays up until the early morning, watching television with the volume low, listening over the dialogue for any sound that might mean someone is entering his home. He checks the locks obsessively. When a delivery is late or a text goes unanswered, his mind jumps to catastrophe: something bad is happening, someone is coming for him.

At work, Duy paints interiors for a small crew. As soon as he enters a new house, he scans every room for exits before he picks up a brush. On a ladder, if a homeowner walks into the room unexpectedly, he freezes completely, unable to move or speak until the person leaves. He is certain that they are watching him, judging him, and that any moment they might turn hostile. The feeling of being observed makes his hands shake so badly that he has ruined two ceilings this month. His boss has noticed and warned him about the mistakes. Duy has started turning down jobs in neighborhoods that remind him of Marcus—the same coffee shops, the same corner stores, the same street where he used to park. He cannot explain why; he just knows that if he sees a car like Marcus’s, his chest goes tight and he needs to leave.

Duy blames himself. He has come to believe that the abuse happened to him because of the sort of person he is—weak, too trusting, inadequate. His current boyfriend, Leo, is gentle and patient, but Duy cannot shake the feeling that he does not belong in a safe relationship either. He feels like a fraud, waiting for Leo to see the same flaws Marcus saw. When Leo asks him what is wrong, Duy freezes again, unable to find the words. At night, he lies still beside Leo, scanning the dark for threats, listening for footsteps that are not there.

What finally brought Duy to therapy was a panic attack in the middle of a job site. He dropped his roller, sat down on the drop cloth, and could not stop shaking. His boss called Leo, who drove him home. That evening, Leo held him and said quietly, "You don't have to carry this alone." Duy is terrified that if he lets himself feel the memory fully, something will break inside him. But he is also desperate to stop scanning every room, to stop checking the locks, to stop believing that he deserved what happened. He does not know how to belong anywhere again, but he has come to this room hoping that someone can help him find a way back.
